title: What Is an NNN Lease
name: What Is an NNN Lease
metaTitle: What Is an NNN Lease for Los Angeles, CA Property
metaDescription: A plain language explanation of what an NNN lease is, common Los Angeles property types that use it, and what a buyer should review before acquiring one.

sections.html: An NNN lease, short for triple net lease, is a commercial lease agreement under which the tenant pays base rent plus the three major operating cost categories: property taxes, building insurance, and common area or building maintenance. For an investor new to commercial real estate, understanding what an NNN lease actually obligates the tenant to pay, and what it leaves with the landlord, is essential before evaluating any Los Angeles property marketed with this lease structure.

sections.heading: Reading the Lease, Not Just the Label
sections.html: The term NNN gets used loosely in marketing materials, and the actual lease document does not always match a textbook triple net structure. Some leases described as NNN still leave the landlord responsible for roof and structural repairs, or cap the tenant's expense reimbursement obligations in certain years. Before treating a Los Angeles property as a true, low involvement net lease investment, a buyer needs to review the actual lease terms line by line rather than relying on how the listing describes the lease.

sections.heading: Common Property Types Leased This Way in Los Angeles
sections.html: NNN leases are common among single tenant retail buildings such as pharmacies, quick service restaurants, and auto parts or convenience stores along major Los Angeles commercial corridors, as well as certain single tenant industrial and office buildings leased to a corporate user. Multi tenant properties can also use net lease structures for individual tenant spaces, though a multi tenant building typically requires more landlord involvement in managing shared common areas even when individual tenant leases are structured on a net basis.

sections.heading: What a Buyer Should Verify Before Closing
sections.html: A prospective buyer of an NNN leased Los Angeles property should confirm the tenant's actual payment history, review the specific expense reimbursement language in the lease, understand any landlord obligations that survive the net structure such as roof or structural repairs, and evaluate the remaining lease term against their own holding period goals. Estoppel certificates from the tenant, confirming the lease terms and that no defaults exist, are a standard part of due diligence on any net lease acquisition.

sections.heading: How This Applies Within a 1031 Exchange
sections.html: For a Los Angeles exchanger, an NNN leased property is a straightforward form of directly owned real property, which qualifies as like kind replacement property under Section 1031 without the additional legal analysis required for DST, TIC, or partnership based structures. We help exchangers identify and evaluate NNN replacement candidates within their identification window, coordinating the due diligence review alongside the exchanger's own legal counsel.

sections.heading: Roof and Structure Responsibility Is the Most Common Landlord Carve Out
sections.html: Even in a lease marketed as triple net, it is common for the landlord to retain responsibility for roof and structural repairs, since tenants are generally unwilling to take on the risk of a major capital item like a roof replacement that may occur after their lease term ends. A Los Angeles buyer should specifically confirm this allocation in the lease document and budget for the possibility of a roof or structural capital expense during their ownership period, rather than assuming the triple net label means zero landlord capital responsibility.

sections.heading: Percentage Rent Clauses in Certain Retail NNN Leases
sections.html: Some retail net leases, particularly for tenants whose sales volume varies significantly, include a percentage rent clause requiring the tenant to pay additional rent based on a percentage of sales above a specified threshold, on top of the base net rent. A Los Angeles buyer evaluating a retail net lease property with a percentage rent clause should review the tenant's actual reported sales history, where available, to understand whether this additional income component is a meaningful and reliable part of the property's total return.

sections.heading: Assignment and Subletting Provisions Affect Long Term Flexibility
sections.html: The lease's provisions governing tenant assignment and subletting affect how much control the landlord retains if the original tenant wants to transfer its interest to another operator, which matters over a long net lease term where a tenant's business circumstances can change. A Los Angeles buyer should review these provisions carefully, since overly permissive assignment language can allow a strong original tenant to be replaced by a weaker one without meaningful landlord consent rights, undermining the credit quality the buyer originally underwrote.

sections.heading: Why Reviewing the Actual Lease Document Is Worth the Time It Takes
sections.html: Because the financial performance of an NNN property depends entirely on the specific obligations spelled out in the lease rather than the general category label, a Los Angeles buyer working within an exchange timeline should still budget time for a legal review of the actual lease document, even under time pressure, rather than relying on a broker's summary alone. We coordinate this review process with the exchanger's legal counsel as part of identifying and closing on a net lease replacement property.

sections.heading: Legal Review Recommended Before Any NNN Purchase
sections.html:
Because the actual obligations under an NNN lease are set by the specific lease document rather than the general NNN label, we recommend every Los Angeles buyer have their attorney review the complete lease agreement before closing on a net lease acquisition, regardless of how the property is marketed. This general overview cannot substitute for that document specific legal review.

Buyers sometimes ask whether an older NNN lease with several renewal option periods already built in is safer than a newer lease with a single long initial term. Both structures have tradeoffs: a lease already into its renewal options shows a demonstrated tenant commitment to the location, while a long initial term newer lease offers more certainty before the first renewal decision point, and reviewing the tenant's actual performance at the location is useful context either way.

faqs.q: Does the term NNN always mean the landlord has zero ongoing expense responsibility?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Some leases marketed as NNN still leave the landlord responsible for certain items like roof or structural repairs, so the actual lease language needs to be reviewed rather than relying on the marketing label.

faqs.q: What is an estoppel certificate and why does it matter in an NNN acquisition?
faqs.a: An estoppel certificate is a document signed by the tenant confirming the current lease terms and that no defaults exist, which protects the buyer from relying on outdated or inaccurate lease information at closing.

faqs.q: What kinds of properties in Los Angeles commonly use NNN leases?
faqs.a: Single tenant retail buildings such as pharmacies and quick service restaurants, along with certain single tenant industrial and office buildings leased to a corporate user, commonly use NNN lease structures.

faqs.q: Does a multi tenant property ever use net lease terms?
faqs.a: Yes, individual tenant spaces within a multi tenant building can be leased on a net basis, though the landlord typically retains more involvement managing shared common areas than in a true single tenant net lease building.

faqs.q: Does an NNN leased property qualify for a 1031 exchange the same way as any other directly owned real property?
faqs.a: Yes, a directly owned NNN leased property is real property held for investment, which qualifies as like kind replacement property under Section 1031 without additional entity structure analysis.
